issues.legal_issue: A testamentary bequest under the applicable traditional Hindu law to a person unborn when the testator died is void, and a direction for future devolution is not a family provision merely because it benefits relatives.
material_facts: The will provided that, after the testator’s death, his brother would enjoy the properties for life and that any sons born to the brother would take the properties after the brother’s death.
The testator died before the brother’s sons were born.
The properties were governed by traditional Hindu law in a territory where the legislation permitting bequests to unborn beneficiaries was not in force at the relevant time.
The disposition set out a future course of devolution to nephews or nieces rather than providing for family support.
issues.conclusion: The bequests to the brother’s sons were void. The court rejected the argument that the provision was a family provision and applied the established rule against bequests to unborn persons under the applicable traditional Hindu law.
issues.legal_principle: In Tagore v. Tagore (1872), I.A. Supp. 47, the Judicial Committee held that a Hindu could not make a gift or bequest to a person not in existence, in fact or in contemplation of law, when the disposition took effect. Although the Court questioned the basis attributed to that rule in Tagore, it applied the maxim communis error facit jus because the rule had long governed property arrangements and titles; it referred to Charles Dalton v. Henry Angus & Co., (1881) 6 A.C. 740 at 812. The Hindu Transfers and Bequests Act, 1914, the Hindu Disposition of Property Act, 1916, and the Hindu Transfers and Bequests (City of Madras) Act, 1921, subject to the limitations in sections 113–116 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, altered the rule in the territories where they applied, but none applied to these properties at the relevant time. The Court held that a direction for future devolution to relatives was not a family provision.

rule.if: will_dispute and traditional_hindu_law_applies and beneficiary_unborn_when_testator_died and disposition_sets_future_devolution

predicates.will_dispute: The proceeding concerns the validity or effect of a disposition made by will.
predicates.traditional_hindu_law_applies: The properties are governed by traditional Hindu law that does not permit a bequest to an unborn beneficiary.
predicates.beneficiary_unborn_when_testator_died: The beneficiary was not in existence when the testator died.
predicates.disposition_sets_future_devolution: The will directs how property is to pass in the future rather than providing for family support.

issues.definition: When a will dispute concerns property governed by traditional Hindu law and a future-devolution bequest to a person unborn at the testator’s death, the bequest is void.

issues.legal_issue: A joint will’s general clause stating that it takes effect after both makers have died does not postpone a disposition that gives the survivor a life interest after the first maker’s death.
material_facts: The two makers executed a joint will containing separate dispositions concerning their respective properties.
For one maker’s properties, the will gave the other maker a life interest, followed by a remainder to the latter’s sons or, in their absence, daughters.
The will also contained a general clause stating that it would take effect after both makers had died.
The life interest was expressly intended to operate after the first maker’s death and during the survivor’s life.
issues.conclusion: The will was not intended to operate only after both makers had died. As to the properties subject to the life interest, the disposition took effect on the first maker’s death and the remainder was not postponed until the survivor’s death for purposes of determining whether the beneficiaries were unborn.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed the will as a whole, giving effect to its distinct dispositions and not allowing an isolated general expression to override the express life interest. Because that life interest was intended to begin after the first maker’s death and endure during the survivor’s life, the general clause could not literally govern every disposition in the will.

predicates.will_interpretation_dispute: The proceeding requires interpretation of a will to determine when a disposition takes effect.
predicates.joint_will_disposes_of_makers_property_s: The joint will makes separate dispositions concerning the property of its makers.
predicates.will_grants_survivor_a_life_interest: The will gives the surviving maker a life interest in the property.
predicates.blanket_clause_says_effect_follows_both_: The will contains a general clause saying that it takes effect only after both makers have died.

issues.definition: Where a joint will separately disposes of its makers’ property, grants the survivor a life interest, and contains a general clause referring to both deaths, the disposition subject to that life interest takes effect on the first maker’s death.

issues.legal_issue: When a will’s gift to one class of beneficiaries is void and its conditional gift to another class fails, the property devolves by intestate succession, subject to proof of the claimants’ status as lawful heirs.
material_facts: The sons named as remainder beneficiaries were unborn when the testator died, so they could not take under the will.
The will gave the daughters a benefit only if the life tenant died leaving no sons.
Male children had been born to the life tenant before his death, and the daughters’ gift was therefore subject to the stated condition concerning sons.
The life tenant died after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applied to the succession in question.
The lower appellate court had not determined whether the claimants were legitimate sons, so that question remained for determination on remand.
issues.conclusion: Neither the sons nor the daughters could take under the will: the sons’ bequest was void and the daughters’ gift failed under its condition. The property therefore devolved by intestate succession under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956; the claimants’ entitlement to a lawful share depended on the determination that they were legitimate sons.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the sons could not take under the will because they were unborn when the testator died, and that the daughters’ bequest was defeasible if the life tenant left sons. With neither class taking under the will, the Court applied the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and recognized the claimants’ lawful share subject to the unresolved question of legitimacy.

rule.if: will_dispute and remainder_beneficiaries_unborn_at_testators_death and daughter_gift_conditioned_on_no_sons_at_life_tenants_death and male_children_born_to_life_tenant and intestacy_law_applies

predicates.will_dispute: The proceeding concerns who takes property disposed of by a will.
predicates.remainder_beneficiaries_unborn_at_testat: The persons named to take the remainder were unborn when the testator died.
predicates.daughter_gift_conditioned_on_no_sons_at_: The will gives the daughters an interest only if the life tenant dies without sons.
predicates.male_children_born_to_life_tenant: Male children were born to the life tenant before his death.
predicates.intestacy_law_applies: The applicable succession law provides for distribution when no beneficiary takes under the will.

issues.definition: When the will’s remainder beneficiaries were unborn at the testator’s death, its conditional gift to daughters fails because male children were born to the life tenant, and intestacy law applies, the property devolves by intestate succession.
